setting.name: Win32 Callout Watchdog Bugcheck Enabled
setting.casual_explanation: This appears to be a low-level watchdog-related value under Session Manager Power. On the current clean baseline, the parent key exists but the value is not configured.
setting.why_people_change_it: Kernel and power researchers may inspect this value when tracing watchdog behavior around Session Manager power initialization and callout handling.
setting.tradeoffs_overview: The value is kernel-adjacent, boot-relevant, and still unproven as an end-user tweak. Evidence is good enough to keep it in the research queue as a watchdog-family adjacent global, but not good enough to apply, recommend, or even treat as the strongest next watchdog candidate without a real seeding or read path. A dedicated KVM Procmon runtime replay reached live guest execution, but it still failed at `Procmon SaveAs` before any CSV review could happen. A later neutral-value VM perf bench covered apply and rollback mechanics without exercising a behavior-changing DWORD `1`.
setting.professional_notes: The current repo evidence says `HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Session Manager\\Power\\Win32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled` is absent by default on the clean baseline while the parent path exists. A later targeted current-build string batch found an exact Unicode hit in `C:\\Windows\\System32\\ntoskrnl.exe`. A later KVM local-KD symbol sweep resolved a live `nt!PopWin32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled` global alongside `PopWatchdogInit`, `PopWatchdogResumeTimeout`, `PopWatchdogSleepTimeout`, and `PopInvokeWin32CalloutWithWatchdog`, which proved the sibling still exists in the current watchdog-family symbol surface. A direct KVM local-KD follow-up then showed that `PopInvokeWin32CalloutWithWatchdog` uses `PopWin32kCalloutWatchdogTimeoutSeconds`, builds a watchdog callback packet around `PopWin32CalloutWatchdogCallback`, calls `ZwPowerInformation`, and then invokes `PsInvokeWin32Callout`; the same pass read `PopWin32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled = 0` live, but did not show that wrapper reading the target global. The new canonical PDB-backed Ghidra full-analysis pass confirmed that the exact value-name string still exists in `ntoskrnl.exe`, but recovered zero direct code xrefs from that string. The new broader KVM local-KD seed sweep then widened the search across watchdog/bugcheck symbols and helper disassembly, but still did not reveal a target-specific setter, copy helper, or registry seeding caller for the global. The only proven current-build registry helper path in this neighborhood remains the generic power reader chain `PopReadUlongPowerKey -> PopReadRegKeyValue -> ZwOpenKey / ZwQueryValueKey`, and the directly observed timeout selector still reads `PopWatchdogSleepTimeout` and `PopWatchdogResumeTimeout`, not this sibling. The right interpretation is now narrower: this is an adjacent watchdog-family global with unproven registry semantics on the current build, not the strongest un-packaged watchdog tweak lead. Absent a new runtime or documentation lead, this sibling should stop taking priority over stronger watchdog lanes. A later host-side current-build INIT descriptor scan then found the `Win32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled` UTF-16 string and one nearby `Session Manager\Power` row at file offset `0xbeda88` pointing at static RVA `0xFC5FA8`, matching the live KD RVA for `nt!PopWin32CalloutWatchdogBugcheckEnabled`. That narrows the open question further: the current build still carries a concrete registry-seeding table entry for the sibling even though the currently observed wrapper/code-xref lanes do not show who consumes it. A dedicated KVM Procmon runtime replay then reused `TriggerProfile = watchdog-power-burst`, reached live guest execution, uploaded a `procmon-saveas` stage marker, and ended with `Procmon SaveAs timed out after 60 second(s).` The result text still reported the restored state as path-missing and value-missing, so the runtime lane now fails as an explicit Procmon export blocker rather than as an unrun or ambiguous trigger lane. A later neutral-value VM perf bench deliberately applied DWORD `0`, matching the live KD-observed global value, to avoid exercising behavior-changing bugcheck semantics. The bench verified apply, measured 3 relative VM samples, restored the missing baseline by deleting the value, and verified rollback. The first bench pass exposed and fixed a PowerShell median-index bug in `run-perf-bench-guest.ps1`; the retained rerun reports baseline median `7.028 ms`, applied median `3.723 ms`, and rollback verified. Those timing numbers are VM-relative and not a performance claim; the useful conclusion is that apply/rollback mechanics are now covered without changing intended bugcheck behavior.
